dicas.texto: Você está indo bem! Se a música tem 6 partes no total, em quantas partes iguais precisamos dividir o espaço entre 0 e 1 na reta?
Tente imaginar 6 espaços iguais entre o 0 e o 1. Onde ficaria a quinta marcação, contando a partir do zero?
Como o denominador é 6, o ponto deve estar bem perto do 1, faltando apenas um 'passo' de tamanho 1/6 para chegar lá.
Divida mentalmente a reta em 6 pedaços. O 5/6 é o quinto ponto. Tente clicar quase no final da reta, um pouco antes do número 1.

solutionTrace.thinking: O enunciado afirma que Jack ouviu 5 minutos de uma música de 6 minutos, logo o numerador é 5.
O tempo total da música é 6 minutos, logo o denominador é 6.

error.howToFix: Relembrar a definição de fração: parte/todo.

interfaceCtat.descricao: Interface FIXA do tutor (a mesma tela para todos os problemas): enunciado; pergunta "What is the fraction in the problem?" com duas caixas numéricas (f1 em cima = numerador, f2 embaixo = denominador); reta numérica de 0 a 1 (numline) onde o aluno marca um ponto, com encaixe em 6 partes por unidade (marcas ocultas); texto de apoio na reta: "The number hint is off in this problem!"; botão Hint; botão Done. Os passos do aluno são ações NESSES componentes (digitar nos campos, converter, marcar o ponto, concluir).

campo numérico: parte inteira do número misto

dicas.texto: Which number represents the part of the song Jack has already listened to?
Use the listened portion as the numerator, the number written above the fraction bar.
Look at the number of minutes Jack has listened to, not the total length of the song.
Enter the listened minutes in the top box of the fraction.
Which number represents the entire song?
Use the total amount as the denominator, the number written below the fraction bar.
The denominator comes from the song's full length, not from the minutes already heard.
Enter the total minutes in the bottom box of the fraction.
Compare the part with the whole. Is the amount listened to smaller than the entire song?
A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator and does not need a whole-number part.
Check whether the top number is less than the bottom number before using the conversion control.
Keep the fraction in its original numerator-over-denominator form when the numerator is less than the denominator.
Think of the distance from 0 to 1 as one whole divided into equal parts.
Use the denominator to determine the number of equal intervals, then count the intervals named by the numerator.
The point should be close to 1 because Jack listened to almost the entire song.
Starting at 0, move through the equal intervals until you have counted the listened portion of the six-part whole.
Ask how many complete songs Jack has finished.
For a proper fraction, determine how many whole units fit completely before identifying the remaining fraction.
Jack has not completed a full second song; he is still describing only part of one song.
Enter the number of complete wholes before the fractional part in the m1 field.

Jack is enjoying a certain song that is 6 minutes long, and he has been listening to it for 5 minutes now. That means he has listened to 5/6 of the song. Show this fraction on the number line.
